summary: Describes a protocol that provides lossless compression for IP datagrams, so packets can be made smaller before being sent.

plainLanguage.summary: IPComp shrinks the data inside an IP packet before it is sent, so the packet takes less room on the wire. The two ends must agree in advance on which algorithm to use, and the compression must be exact: the packet that comes out has to be identical to the one that went in.

questions: how does ip payload compression work
what is a compression parameter index
subtitle: How to shrink IP packet payloads before sending, and how two nodes agree to do it.

tldr.problem: Large IP packets cost more to send over a slow or congested link, and encryption makes the data incompressible, so compression has to happen before the encryption is applied.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IPComp protocol, a four-octet header inserted before the compressed payload, and the IPComp Association, which records the algorithm and its parameters for a pair of nodes. The IP header is rewritten to mark the packet as protocol 108.
tldr.outcome: Payloads travel smaller when that helps, and uncompressed when it does not, so a packet never grows. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2393.

today: RFC 3173 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2001. It obsoletes RFC 2393, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IPComp Does
sections.content:
IP payload compression is a protocol to reduce the size of IP datagrams. The RFC says it will increase the overall communication performance between a pair of communicating hosts or gateways, the nodes, by compressing the datagrams, provided the nodes have sufficient computation power through either CPU capacity or a compression coprocessor, and the communication is over slow or congested links.

IP payload compression is especially useful when encryption is applied to IP datagrams. Encrypting the IP datagram causes the data to be random in nature, which renders compression at lower protocol layers, such as the PPP Compression Control Protocol of RFC 1962, ineffective. If both compression and encryption are required, compression must be applied before encryption.

The document defines the IP payload compression protocol itself, the IPComp packet structure, the IPComp Association, and several methods to negotiate the association. Other documents specify how a specific compression algorithm can be used with the protocol; those algorithms are beyond the scope of this document, and no compression algorithm is mandatory for an implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: IPComp shrinks the data inside an IP packet before it is sent, so the packet takes less room on the wire. The two ends must agree in advance on which algorithm to use, and the compression must be exact: the packet that comes out has to be identical to the one that went in.

sections.title: The Compression Process and Its Ordering
sections.content:
The compression processing of IP datagrams has two phases: compressing outbound datagrams and decompressing inbound ones. It MUST be lossless, ensuring that the IP datagram, after being compressed and decompressed, is identical to the original.

Each IP datagram is compressed and decompressed by itself, without any relation to other datagrams, which the RFC calls stateless compression, because IP datagrams may arrive out of order or not arrive at all. Each compressed IP datagram encapsulates a single IP payload. Processing of inbound datagrams MUST support both compressed and non-compressed datagrams, to meet the non-expansion policy requirements of Section 2.2.

The ordering matters. Compression of outbound datagrams MUST be done before any IP security processing, such as encryption and authentication, and before any fragmentation of the IP datagram. In IP version 6 (RFC 2460), it MUST also be done before the addition of either a Hop-by-Hop Options header or a Routing Header, since both carry information that must be examined and processed by possibly every node along the packet's delivery path and therefore MUST be sent in the original form.

Decompression of inbound datagrams MUST be done after the reassembly of the datagrams and after the completion of all IP security processing, such as authentication and decryption.

Section 2.1 defines what is compressed. The compression is applied to a single array of octets that are contiguous in the IP datagram and that always ends at the last octet of the IP packet payload. In IP version 4 (RFC 791) the compression is applied to the payload, starting at the first octet following the IP header and continuing through the last octet of the datagram, and no portion of the IP header or its options is compressed. In the case of an encapsulated IP header, such as tunnel mode encapsulation in IPsec, the payload is defined to start immediately after the outer IP header, so the inner IP header is considered part of the payload and is compressed.

In the IPv6 context, IPComp is viewed as an end-to-end payload and MUST NOT apply to hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers. The compression starts at the first IP Header Option field that does not carry information that must be examined and processed by nodes along the delivery path, if such a field exists, and continues to the upper layer payload. The size of a compressed payload MUST be in whole octet units.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is compressed on its own, with no memory of the packets before it, because IP packets can arrive out of order or not at all. On the way out the payload is compressed first, then the IP security processing such as encryption is applied, and only then is the packet fragmented. On the way in the order is reversed.

sections.title: The Non-Expansion Policy
sections.content:
Compression does not always make a datagram smaller, and a policy is needed so that it never makes things worse. If the total size of a compressed payload and the IPComp header is not smaller than the size of the original payload, the IP datagram MUST be sent in the original non-compressed form, with no IPComp header added. The RFC gives the reasons: the policy saves the decompression processing cycles and avoids incurring IP datagram fragmentation when the expanded datagram is larger than the MTU.

Small IP datagrams are likely to expand as a result of compression, so a numeric threshold should be applied before compression, with datagrams smaller than the threshold sent in the original form without attempting compression. The threshold is implementation dependent.

An IP datagram with a payload that has been previously compressed tends not to compress any further. The previously compressed payload may be the result of external processes, such as compression applied by an upper layer in the communication stack or by an offline compression utility. An adaptive algorithm should be implemented to avoid the performance hit. The RFC's example is that if the compression of i consecutive datagrams of an association fails, the next several datagrams, say k, are sent without attempting compression; if the next j datagrams also fail to compress, a larger number, say k+n, are sent uncompressed; and once a datagram is compressed successfully, the normal process restarts. Such an adaptive algorithm, and all its thresholds, is implementation dependent.

During the processing of the payload, the compression algorithm MAY periodically apply a test to determine the compressibility of the processed data, similar to the requirements of Recommendation V.42 bis. Once the algorithm detects that the data is non-compressible, it SHOULD stop processing the data and the payload is sent in the original non-compressed form.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression does not always make a packet smaller. A small packet can grow, and data that was already compressed cannot be compressed again. So the rules are: if the compressed version is not smaller than the original, send the original; and if compression keeps failing, the sender should stop trying for a while and send the data uncompressed.

sections.title: The IPComp Header and the IP Header Changes
sections.content:
A compressed IP datagram is encapsulated by modifying the IP header and inserting an IPComp header immediately preceding the compressed payload. The IPComp header is a four-octet structure with three fields.

Next Header is an 8-bit selector that stores the IPv4 Protocol field or the IPv6 Next Header field of the original IP header. Flags is an 8-bit field reserved for future use, which MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiving node. Compression Parameter Index is a 16-bit index stored in network order.

The CPI values are divided into ranges. The values 0 to 63 designate well-known compression algorithms, which require no additional information and are used for manual setup, and the values themselves are identical to the IPCOMP Transform identifiers defined in RFC 2407. The values 64 to 255 are reserved for future use. The values 256 to 61439 are negotiated between the two nodes when an association is defined. The values 61440 to 65535 are for private use among mutually consenting parties.

Both nodes participating can select a CPI value independently of each other, and there is no relationship between the two separately chosen values. The outbound IPComp header MUST use the CPI value chosen by the decompressing node. The CPI in combination with the destination IP address uniquely identifies the compression algorithm characteristics for the datagram. When negotiating one of the well-known algorithms, the nodes MAY select a CPI in the predefined range 0 to 63.

The IP header changes are as follows. In IPv4, the Total Length is set to the length of the entire encapsulated datagram, including the IP header, the IPComp header and the compressed payload, the Protocol field is set to 108, IPComp Datagram, and the Header Checksum is recomputed. All other IPv4 header fields are kept unchanged, including any header options. In IPv6, the Payload Length is set to the length of the compressed IP payload and the Next Header field is set to 108. All other IPv6 header fields are kept unchanged, including any non-compressed header options. The IPComp header is placed in an IPv6 packet using the same rules as the IPv6 Fragment Header, but if a packet contains both a Fragment Header and an IPComp header, the Fragment Header MUST precede the IPComp header.

On decompression, the array of octets starts immediately after the IPComp header and ends at the last octet of the IP payload. If the decompression succeeds, the IP header is modified to indicate the size of the decompressed datagram and the original next header, the IPComp header is removed, and the decompressed payload immediately follows the IP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressed packet has a small four-byte header inserted in front of the data. It holds the original value of the protocol field, a reserved byte, and a 16-bit number that says which compression algorithm was used. The IP header itself is changed to say that the packet now holds an IPComp datagram, using protocol number 108.

sections.title: Negotiating the IPComp Association
sections.content:
To use the protocol, two nodes MUST first establish an IPComp Association between them. The association includes all the information required for the operation of IPComp: the Compression Parameter Index, the mode of operation, the compression algorithm to be used, and any required parameter for the selected algorithm.

The policy for establishing IPComp may be either a node-to-node policy, where IPComp is applied to every IP packet between the nodes, or a session-based policy, where only selected sessions between the nodes employ it. Two nodes may choose to negotiate IPComp in either or both directions, and they may choose to employ a different compression algorithm in each direction, but they MUST negotiate a compression algorithm in each direction for which they establish an association, because there is no default compression algorithm.

The association is established by dynamic negotiation or by manual configuration. The dynamic negotiations SHOULD use the Internet Key Exchange protocol (RFC 2409) where IPsec is present, and MAY be implemented through a different protocol, which is beyond the scope of the document. Manual configuration designates a limited number of Compression Parameter Indexes to represent a list of specific compression methods.

With IKE, the association is negotiated by the initiator using a Proposal Payload containing one or more Transform Payloads. The Proposal Payload specifies the IP Payload Compression Protocol in the protocol ID field, and each Transform Payload contains the specific compression algorithm being offered to the responder. The CPI is sent in the SPI field of the proposal with the SPI size field set to match: it SHOULD be sent as a 16-bit number with the SPI size field set to 2, and MAY be sent as a 32-bit value with the size field set to 4, in which case the 16-bit CPI MUST be placed in the two least significant octets and the two most significant octets MUST be zero and ignored by the receiving node. The receiving node MUST be able to process both forms.

Two attributes are applicable to IPComp proposals. To propose a non-default Encapsulation Mode, such as Tunnel Mode, a proposal MUST include an Encapsulation Mode attribute, and if the mode is unspecified the default is Transport Mode. The Lifetime attribute, using the Life Duration and Life Type attributes, suggests a life duration for the association. When IPComp is negotiated as part of a Protection Suite, an IPComp proposal MUST NOT be rejected for lacking attributes of other protocols in the suite that are not relevant to IPComp, and such attributes MUST be ignored when setting the association and in its operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any of this can happen the two nodes must set up an association, which records the algorithm, its settings, and which number will name it on the wire. They can configure it by hand, or negotiate it dynamically, and the RFC recommends using the Internet Key Exchange protocol when IP security is in use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When IPComp is used in the context of IPsec, it is believed not to have an effect on the underlying security functionality provided by the IPsec protocol. The use of compression is not known to degrade or alter the nature of the underlying security architecture or the encryption technologies used to implement it.

When IPComp is used without IPsec, IP payload compression potentially reduces the security of the Internet, in a way similar to the effects of IP encapsulation (RFC 2003). The RFC's example is that IPComp may make it difficult for border routers to filter datagrams based on header fields. In particular, the original value of the Protocol field in the IP header is not located in its normal position within the datagram, and any transport layer header fields within the datagram, such as port numbers, are neither located in their normal positions nor presented in their original values after compression.

A filtering border router can filter the datagram only if it shares the IPComp Association used for the compression. To allow this sort of compression in environments in which all packets need to be filtered, or at least accounted for, a mechanism must be in place for the receiving node to securely communicate the association to the border router. The RFC notes that this might, more rarely, also apply to the association used for outgoing datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Used with IP security, compression is not known to weaken the encryption. Used on its own, it can make it harder for a border router to filter packets, because the fields a filter looks at are no longer where they were.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2393
sections.content:
Section 7 of the RFC summarizes the changes from RFC 2393 that an implementer should be aware of. All the changes are meant to clarify the negotiation of an IPComp Association using IKE in the context of IPsec.

  • IPComp can be negotiated stand-alone or bundled with other protocols in a Protection Suite.
  • The CPI is defined in the SPI field of an IKE proposal: a two-octet field is a SHOULD and a four-octet field a MAY, with the placement of the 16-bit CPI in the four-octet form specified and a receiver required to process both field sizes.
  • The default Encapsulation Mode is defined as Transport Mode, and a proposal is required to include an Encapsulation Mode attribute when it suggests a non-default encapsulation such as Tunnel Mode.
  • The Lifetime attribute is added to the list of supported attributes, along with Transport Mode.
  • Attributes of transforms in a Protection Suite that are not applicable to IPComp should not be included in an IPComp proposal and must be ignored when setting the association and in its operation. IPComp implementations must never reject a proposal for lacking such attributes.
  • Implementation notes on negotiating and using CPIs in the predefined, well-known range were added.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition is the same protocol as the earlier one, with the negotiation rules spelled out more precisely: how the compression parameter index is carried, what the default encapsulation mode is, and how attributes that belong to other protocols are handled.
